To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Fe(III) isotopic signature and Fe concentrations of carbonates and associated mudrocks of Neoarchean shelf facies of South Africa are the result of a complex interplay of depositional and diagenetic processes, and that the Fe(2+) concentration and isotope composition of the shallow marine environment was likely controlled by the oxidation and precipitation of Fe(2+).

Fe(II)-aq in the Archean ocean was likely 10 to 100 times higher than today, that Fe(II)aq was removed from the ocean water column by shallow shelf oxidation, and that Fe(III)-poorly soluble minerals were formed and deposited on the shallow continental shelf, whereas Fe(III) minerals were deposited on the slope.

Fe isotope compositions and concentrations of carbonate rocks from the Neoarchaeon Campbellrand-Malman carbonate platform (CMPC) in South Africa indicate the presence of molecular O2 in shallow marine settings, and that Fe(IIaq) content in the water column was lower on the shelf than in deeper water.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reconstruction of the Fe cycle in the Archean ocean, in particular the role of shallow-marine oxygen production and its impact on the Fe cycle.
the reconstruction of the Fe cycle in Neoarchean shallow marine systems and its relationship with the rise of oxygen in the atmosphere.
the reconstruction of the iron cycle in the Neoarchean open ocean.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Fe isotope systematics of carbonates deposited in open marine settings can be used to reconstruct the Fe cycle in the water column and that carbonates from peritidal settings are more likely affected by early diagenesis.
the Fe cycle of the Neoarchean ocean was not dominated by the continental shelves, but by the open ocean.

the Fe isotope systematics of the CMCP carbonates are consistent with a shallow marine Fe cycle that was already influenced by oxygen production, but that the exact nature of the oxygen source remains unclear and requires further investigation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Neoarchean marine Fe cycle was likely more complex and heterogeneous than previously thought.
the Neoarchean ocean was not only ferruginous, but also oxygenated.
the Neoarchean ocean was not as ferruginous as previously thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Fe cycle in shallow marine settings was likely different to the Fe cycle in the open ocean.

the Fe isotope systematics of carbonates are sensitive to the depositional environment and the presence of Fe-bearing minerals in adjacent sediments, and that Fe isotope signatures of pure carbonates can be used to reconstruct Fe cycling and redox conditions in ancient seawater.
the marine Fe cycle was not uniform along the Neoarchen Campbellrand-Malani carbonate platform.
